newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland's centre-right allies in narrow poll win.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's centre-right allies in narrow poll win.

text.p: The centre-right opposition of Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail and the Progressive Democrats won Ireland's election on Sunday but will need the backing of Independents to control a majority in parliament.
Final results showed the pairing winning a total of 81 seats in the 166-place parliament, two short of the barest majority it needed to govern without enlisting outside support.
The speaker of the house is neutral and Ahern and his allies needed just 83 seats to claim a majority in the house.
The election ended Prime Minister John Bruton's 30-month-old centre-left "Rainbow Coalition" which presided over an economic boom which created more than 1,000 jobs a month.

Ahern said he was confident that parliament would elect him as Ireland's youngest Prime Minister at the age of 45 when it reconvenes on June 26 but refused to be drawn on the support he would need to carry out policies to cut crime and taxes.

Both he and Bruton had ruled out any electoral survival pact with Sinn Fein, the political wing of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas, which won one seat and will take its place in the Dublin assembly for the first time since the 1920s.

Financial experts said the absence of a clear-cut result was the least attractive outcome but doubted it would unsettle Irish or international markets, which are focused on domestic currency concerns and a possible delay in the EMU start date.

"While it was the least favoured outcome and will create uncertainty, market reaction will be muted and focus will remain on EMU and currency worries," said Pat O'Sullivan, economist with Dublin's AIB capital markets.
Fianna Fail, the nation's most potent political force with 68 seats in the current assembly won 77 seats against 54 captured by Bruton's Christian Democrat Fine Gael party, its main political rival.
But Ahern's prospects of heading a strong right of centre government were dented by the mauling Mary Harney's Progressive Democrats took at the hands of voters.
The PDs won only four seats against eight in the current parliament in a backlash against her plans to cut 25,000 civil service jobs and make single mothers stay in the parental home.
Bruton's hopes suffered a similar setback when his Labour party ally of Dick Spring was spurned by voters, who trimmed its representation in parliament from 32 to 17 seats.

There was speculation that Spring, Ireland's best-known political figure on the world stage, was punished at the polls for ditching a Fianna Fail government in 1994 and switching his votes to Bruton and his junior Democratic Left ally.

Ahern, who heartened financial markets with a pledge to keep government spending to a limit of four per cent, two points over inflation, will find natural allies among the seven Indepndent candidates, political analysts said.
Some are known Fianna Fail sympathisers who broke away to form regional, often rural parties with local agenda which Ahern will be asked to help in return for their backing.

Ahern told reporters that settlement of the Northern Ireland conflict, which has killed 3,200 people in 28 years, would be a priority and said the opportunity for progress created by the election of a strong new British government was "tremendous."
"The possibilities of moving forward are tremendous," said Ahern who plans to meet Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams this week while he is still in opposition and not yet Prime Minister.

Britain, Ireland and the United States refuse top-level contact with Sinn Fein until its IRA backers restore a truce they broke in February last year when they resumed their war against British rule of Northern Ireland with a London bomb.
Sinn Fein's Caoimhghin O Caolain won a seat in the border constituency of Cavan Monaghan and will occupy it after the party ended a policy of boycotting the house in 1986.
The win followed Sinn Fein's 16 per cent votes in Britain's May 1 poll which elected Adams and chief lieutenant Martin McGuinness to the British parliament.
They are boycotting the British assembly because it would entail an oath of allegiance to Britain.
Sinn Fein says its electoral successes should give it automatic entry to Northern Ireland peace talks in Belfast but Britain and Ireland say it will be barred until a new IRA truce.
